claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory alloy.
The as-cast alloy has coarse, equiaxed grains.
The baseline yield strength is approximately 786 MPa.
The baseline compressive strength is approximately 1314 MPa.
The baseline terminal tensile strain is approximately 13.5%.
A high-temperature solution anneal at approximately 1500 °C under inert atmosphere will homogenize HfZrTiTa0.53.
Approximately 50% cold rolling at room temperature and about 10^-3 s^-1 will introduce stored strain into the alloy.
Recrystallization annealing at approximately 900 °C for 5–10 minutes after cold rolling will produce a bimodal distribution of fine and coarse grains.
The fine-grained matrix will promote uniform plastic deformation during tensile loading.
Fine grains will promote grain-boundary sliding under room-temperature tensile loading.
The fine-grained fraction will delay tensile necking and crack initiation.
The coarse-grained fraction will act as stable load-bearing elements that preserve high strength.
The coarse-grained fraction will preserve impact-triggered energy release.
Processing will increase tensile uniform elongation by 30–50%, from about 13.5% to about 17.5–20%.
Yield strength will remain within approximately ±10% of the baseline value.
Compressive strength will remain within approximately ±10% of the baseline value.
Impact-triggered energy release will not degrade relative to the as-cast baseline.
The ductility hypothesis applies at room temperature under quasi-static loading near 10^-3 s^-1.
The impact comparison applies to loads similar to thin-steel-target penetration tests.
The cited thermomechanical-treatment study provides precedent for homogenization followed by room-temperature cold rolling and rapid annealing.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% baseline is called terminal tensile strain but is then used as the baseline for uniform elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct tensile metrics, so the stated 30–50% comparison is not consistently defined.

The blanket strain-rate condition near 10^-3 s^-1 is presented alongside thin-steel-target penetration impact testing, which is dynamic rather than quasi-static; no separate impact strain-rate or velocity range is specified.
